figures.caption: Overall performance. Left: WorkBuddy-Bench by domain for Gemini 3.5 Flash under OpenCode. Harness2 with parallel recursion at $k{=}5$ exceeds the strongest baseline in every domain, Meta-Harness, and the number above each Harness2 bar is its gain over the base harness. Right: on WB-code, Harness2 keeps improving as the budget $k$ grows.

citing_sentences: Parallel recursion adds up to $3.9$ points on WorkBuddy-Bench, $4.2$ on JobBench, and $6.7$ percentage points on LAB Partial (Figure 1); the budget study shows gains from both parallel and sequential recursion.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: The eight harness components in Harness2, grouped by their role in the runtime.

citing_sentences: Figure 2 shows their runtime roles, and Table 5 in Appendix D.3 lists their files, activation, and definitions.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: The Harness2 pipeline. Task-level recursion proposes invariant and domain-specific harness edits, probes their effects, and composes a successor execution harness. After each task, harnessing-level recursion updates the improvement harness with reusable harnesses and lessons from the refinement process.
figures.headline: The Harness2 pipeline refines the execution harness per task, while a separate improvement harness is updated after each task from reusable harnesses and lessons.
citing_sentences: In Harness2, as shown in Figure 3, the execution harness is refined for the current task, while the continual improvement harness supports refinement across tasks.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Two forms of task-level recursion. (a) Parallel recursion probes multiple candidates and independently composes successor harnesses. (b) Sequential recursion carries each refined harness and accumulated execution evidence into the next step.
figures.headline: Parallel recursion composes successors from a shared candidate pool, while sequential recursion chains each refined harness into the next step.
citing_sentences: Building on the contrastive improvement step, we introduce two forms of task-level recursion (Figure 4): parallel recursion composes refinements from multiple candidate harnesses and their executions, while sequential recursion carries the refined harness and execution evidence into subsequent steps.

figures.caption: Effect of task-level recursion. Performance comparison on WB-code and WB-office as the scaling budget $k$ increases.
figures.headline: Both recursive forms of Harness2 rise monotonically from k=1 to k=5 on WorkBuddy-Bench Code and Office, while Harness Scaling regresses.
citing_sentences: Figure 5 compares parallel and sequential recursion on WB-code and WB-office.

figures.caption: Compute–performance trade-off on JobBench and WorkBuddy-Bench.

citing_sentences: Figure 6 compares performance and total compute on JobBench and WorkBuddy-Bench, counting all tokens spent before the final deliverable is submitted.

citing_sentences: Libraries accumulated with a larger recursion budget support stronger subsequent harness edits even without additional probing, and a library transferred from JobBench improves performance on WorkBuddy-Bench (Figure 7).
Figure 7 examines this connection using libraries accumulated under different recursion budgets.
Figure 7 (left) shows that directly refining the base execution harness without access to reference executions, candidate probes, or the improvement library degrades performance on Code and Web.

abstract: LLM agents’ capabilities depend not only on their underlying models but also on their execution harnesses. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a promising approach to automatically evolve these harnesses. However, deploying RSI in open-world settings still faces two critical challenges. First, open-world tasks are typically unseen during the harness design phase and novel at test time, leaving no ground-truth verifiers to reliably guide online harness edits. Second, the RSI process remains highly task-specific and fails to generalize to novel scenarios. We introduce Harness2, a plug-and-play, recursive agent harnessing framework that addresses these challenges through two connected levels of recursion. Task-level recursion refines the current task’s harness using a contrastive Propose–Probe–Compose step that reliably guides edits without ground-truth verifiers, and can be scaled further via parallel or sequential recursion. Harnessing-level recursion then extracts experience from these edits to update a continual improvement harness, enabling the agent to better adapt to future tasks. Across three professional benchmarks and four model–harness configurations, a single step consistently improves GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash over their base harnesses, yielding gains of up to 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench, 4.5 points on JobBench, and 11.8 percentage points on LAB, with further gains as the task-level recursion budget increases.

sections.body: The introduction defines a harness as the prompts, memory, skills, tools, and orchestration around a model, and argues that harness design must now cover diverse office and legal tasks. It names two challenges for open-world harness evolution: tasks usually lack ground-truth labels or reliable verifiers, and refining a harness for one task does not automatically improve the next. Harness2 responds with task-level recursion, a contrastive Propose–Probe–Compose step that can run in parallel or sequentially, and harnessing-level recursion that updates a library of adopted harnesses and lessons. The section reports that one contrastive step improves all three benchmarks in every configuration, with gains of up to 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench, 4.5 points on JobBench, and 11.8 percentage points in LAB Partial pass rate.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Harness2 targets open-world agent harness evolution, which lacks ground-truth verifiers and fails to transfer across tasks.

sections.body: Harness2 treats the harness as eight editable components: a system prompt, guardrails, memory, skills, tool guidance, scripts, subagents, and a middleware plugin, mounted as files around a frozen model. Task-level recursion runs a contrastive step. It samples a reference execution, proposes an invariant and a domain-specific candidate, probes each under matched conditions, and composes a successor from the behavioral contrasts. Parallel recursion composes k successors from a shared pool, and sequential recursion chains k steps. After each task, harnessing-level recursion keeps the adopted harness and the lessons supported by execution contrasts in a library. The section states a limit: the contrasts inform composition rather than verify correctness, because execution stochasticity and shared model biases limit their reliability.
sections.heading: Harness2
sections.headline: Harness2 pairs task-level recursion, which refines the current harness without verifiers, with a library that carries lessons to later tasks.

sections.body: The section sets up three benchmarks: WorkBuddy-Bench with Code, Web, and Office domains, JobBench, and LAB, reported as Partial per-criterion pass rate. Each result is the mean over three runs with shuffled task order, and #Steps records execution steps per task. Baselines are the base harness, ReasoningBank, Meta-Harness, which searches on a training split offline, and Harness Scaling. Gemini 3.5 Flash and GLM-5 are frozen executors under OpenCode and Codex, with Claude Opus 4.8 as editor. A single step raises GLM-5's average by 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench under OpenCode, and gains reach 4.5 points on JobBench and 11.8 percentage points on LAB Partial. ReasoningBank falls as much as 6.6 points below the base harness on coding tasks. Parallel recursion at k=5 adds 2.9 to 3.9 points on WorkBuddy-Bench. The section notes that recursion does not uniformly close the gap between initial harnesses.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Single-step Harness2 exceeds the base harness on all three benchmarks for GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash under both initial harnesses.

sections.body: Parallel recursion rises from 76.5 to 80.8 on Code and from 79.5 to 83.4 on Office as k grows from 1 to 5, while Harness Scaling regresses from k=2 to k=3. With Gemini 3.5 Flash under OpenCode, k=5 raises the gain over the base from 4.5 to 7.5 points on JobBench and from 5.1 to 8.4 on WorkBuddy-Bench. The ablation at k=1 shows that removing the library lowers WorkBuddy-Bench from 77.5 to 74.4 and JobBench from 36.0 to 34.2. Removing scoping gives 74.6 and 32.3, and removing composition gives 75.9 and 34.1. A library built at k=5 gives gains of 0.9, 4.4, and 5.1 points on Code, Web, and Office without further probing. The cross-task reuse test is retrospective, so it does not measure online adaptation.
sections.heading: Analysis
sections.headline: Score gains grow with recursion budget, and each ablated component lowers WorkBuddy-Bench and JobBench scores.

sections.body: This section places Harness2 among recursive self-improvement methods, which change model weights, improvement programs, or agent code, and among harness optimization methods. Offline methods search candidate harnesses on reusable training tasks using evaluation feedback. Test-time methods refine a task-specific harness through execution feedback, or carry an evolving harness across unlabeled batches, and some use delayed task-outcome feedback. The section describes these systems as utility-, benchmark-, or validation-guided optimization. Harness2 instead accumulates harness improvement across a deployment task stream, without ground-truth feedback, without revisiting completed tasks, and without model updates. The section reports no experiments, and Table 4 summarizes the distinctions.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Harness2 differs from prior harness optimization by learning from its own refinements across a task stream without ground-truth feedback.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the framework. Task-level recursion builds on a contrastive improvement step through parallel composition or sequential refinement. Harnessing-level recursion updates the improvement harness with adopted harnesses and experience from their refinement. The section reports consistent gains over base configurations across three professional benchmarks, two executors, and two initial harnesses. It credits the ablation and transfer studies with showing the value of scoped proposals, composition, and accumulated experience. The section presents recursive harnessing as a foundation for online test-time adaptation across open-world tasks, and it adds no new measurements.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Harness2 turns task-specific refinement into reusable experience, with gains reported across three benchmarks, two executors, and two initial harnesses.

sections.body: The appendix defines six comparison criteria for Table 4: Object, Stage, Label, Streaming, Scaling, and Improver Update, and places Harness2 against prior harness methods. Appendix B gives the benchmark splits: WorkBuddy-Bench test halves of 40, 35, and 25 tasks, a JobBench split with 34 test tasks, and 100 LAB test tasks. Appendix C describes the baselines. An appendix table reports tool-call error rates falling on all three benchmarks, most on JobBench, from 14.4% to 9.1%. Appendix F states limits: recursion adds inference cost over a bounded range of budgets, and behavioral contrasts remain sensitive to execution variability and shared model biases. The appendix also lists the editor, composer, selector, and reflector prompts.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix covers comparison criteria, benchmark splits, baselines, tool-call errors, production harness comparison, failure cases, limitations, and prompts.
